status: PROPOSED — NOT REVIEWED, NOT LOADED AT RUNTIME
drafted_by: Claude (not a Kiswahili or Sheng speaker)
notes: Candidate terms for the SRH scope. The live lexicon carries a named reviewer and a version; terms drafted by a non-speaker do not inherit that, so these sit here until a Kenyan reviewer promotes them.

Two kinds of entry. Most are NORMALISATION ONLY -- they carry no risk tag and exist so that a message written in Kenyan register reaches the English patterns and the corpus vocabulary. A minority carry risk tags, and those are the ones that most need a speaker's judgement, because a wrong risk tag either misses a disclosure or fires the safety path at a girl who asked an ordinary question.

Confidence is marked per term. 'standard' means ordinary Kiswahili I am reasonably confident of; 'sheng' means slang whose current usage varies by year, neighbourhood and age and which I am least able to verify.
Reviewer: please delete anything wrong rather than correcting it politely. A term that does not fire is a smaller problem than one that fires on the wrong thing.

terms.note: mpira is literally 'rubber' and is common; CD is reported slang and is the least certain entry here.
P2 is a Kenyan brand name used generically. Worth confirming it is still the common term.

The one term with measured evidence behind it. Experiment 2: 'inaharibu mji wa mtoto' retrieved a policy report, while its English twin -- contraception damaging the womb -- retrieved the myth-correcting passages immediately. Normalising this is what closes that gap.

terms.meaning: to damage the womb / to close the womb -- a fertility myth about contraception
terms.note: A misconception, not a risk. It should raise the myth-correcting passages, not the safety path.
A support cue, not a risk one. Currently handled by an inline English-side pattern; belongs here instead.

terms.meaning: I have no one to tell
he does not want me to use it / he forbids me
terms.note: Reproductive coercion: pressure not to use a method. Needs a speaker's judgement -- this is the family where a wrong tag has the highest cost in both directions.

terms.meaning: he refuses to use a condom
terms.note: Refusal alone is a preference, not coercion -- the English rules deliberately route 'my boyfriend doesn't like condoms' to support. Tagged possible_coercion rather than reproductive_coercion so it raises scrutiny without deciding. Reviewer should confirm this is the right strength.

terms.meaning: he will leave me / if he leaves me
terms.note: No tag on its own -- fear of abandonment is a support turn. It becomes coercion only when attached to stopping a method, which the English rules already handle as a pair.

terms.meaning: he has forced me / is forcing me
terms.note: Complements 'ananiforce', which is already in the live lexicon.
